```{r setup, include = FALSE}
run = all(vapply(c("mlr3learners", "xgboost", "glmnet"), requireNamespace, logical(1L), quietly = TRUE))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = run)
num = function(x, digits = 3L) if (run) formatC(signif(x, digits), digits = digits, format = "fg", flag = "#") else "?"
txt = function(x) if (run) x else "?"
# mlr3::benchmark() evaluates the fits with the future framework, which attaches the package future; attaching it
# here keeps messages about the installation, such as a package built under another R version, out of the output.
if (run) suppressWarnings(suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(future)))
```

An explanation of a fitted model, such as permutation feature importance (PFI), suggests a conclusion: "the model
relies mainly on these two predictors." Claim-Scoped Diagnostic Gates (CSDG) adds one question before such a conclusion
is reported: does the evidence support this claim? The answer follows five steps: write the claim (Step 1), specify
its scope (Step 2), derive the properties it requires (Step 3), evaluate the evidence for each (Step 4), and decide
and report (Step 5). This vignette runs the steps in the order of an ordinary analysis on a simulated survey.
`r if (!run) "The code is not run because the suggested packages mlr3learners, xgboost, or glmnet are not installed."`

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(mlr3autoiml)
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)
library(data.table)
```

## The analysis

The simulated survey has 1,000 respondents, 12 items, and a binary outcome, `low_wellbeing`. Two scale scores,
`low_mood` and `fatigue`, predict it strongly, and their combination raises the risk more than either alone (an
interaction). `worry_a` and `worry_b` are two wordings of one 5-point worry item with nearly identical answers;
`poor_sleep`, `stress`, and `loneliness` have weak effects; the other five items have none.

```{r data}
simulate_survey = function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  items = c("low_mood", "fatigue", "worry_a", "worry_b", "poor_sleep", "stress", "loneliness", "inactivity",
    "appetite", "concentration", "support", "optimism")
  x = as.data.table(matrix(rnorm(n * 12), n, 12, dimnames = list(NULL, items)))
  worry = rnorm(n)
  # two wordings of the same 5-point worry item; 2% of respondents answer them one category apart
  x[, worry_a := as.integer(cut(worry + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3), c(-Inf, -1.2, -0.4, 0.4, 1.2, Inf)))]
  x[, worry_b := pmin(5L, pmax(1L, worry_a + ifelse(runif(n) < 0.02, sample(c(-1L, 1L), n, TRUE), 0L)))]
  eta = -0.5 + 1.2 * x$low_mood + 1.1 * x$fatigue + 1.5 * x$low_mood * x$fatigue + 0.7 * worry +
    0.5 * x$poor_sleep + 0.2 * x$stress + 0.15 * x$loneliness
  x[, low_wellbeing := factor(rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta)), levels = c(0, 1))]
  as_task_classif(x, target = "low_wellbeing", positive = "1", id = "survey")
}
task = simulate_survey(1000L, seed = 3L)
```

`csdg_fit()` fits XGBoost and ridge logistic regression with `mlr3::benchmark()` on the same ten cross-validation
splits, together with a model without predictors. Log loss serves as the loss for the fold scores, for PFI, and for
the improvement over the model without predictors.

```{r fit}
learners = list(
  xgboost = lrn("classif.xgboost", nrounds = 100, eta = 0.1, max_depth = 3, predict_type = "prob"),
  ridge = lrn("classif.cv_glmnet", alpha = 0, nfolds = 5, predict_type = "prob")
)
fits = csdg_fit(task, learners, folds = 10, seed = 1)
fits
```

```{r fit-assert, include = FALSE}
loss = vapply(fits$resamples, function(r) mean(r$fold_scores$classif.logloss), numeric(1L))
stopifnot(loss[["xgboost"]] < loss[["ridge"]])
```

XGBoost predicts better on held-out data than ridge logistic regression (log loss `r num(loss[["xgboost"]])` versus
`r num(loss[["ridge"]])`), because it can represent the interaction, so its explanation is the one worth reporting.
`csdg_importance()` computes held-out PFI, the increase in held-out log loss when one predictor is permuted, in each
fold with 20 permutations.

```{r importance, fig.alt = "Bar chart of the mean held-out PFI of the leading predictors per learner, with fold values as points and the minimum importance as a dashed line."}
imp = csdg_importance(fits, repetitions = 20, seed = 2)
imp
plot(imp)
```

For each learner, the printout gives the improvement over the model without predictors and 1% of it, the default
minimum importance, in log-loss units; PFI values are not parts of the improvement, so they are compared with it in
these units rather than as shares. The intervals are corrected resampled 95% intervals. In the plot, the bars are
averages over folds, the points are folds, and the dashed line marks the minimum importance.

## Steps 1 and 2: the claim and its scope

The result suggests that XGBoost relies mainly on `fatigue` and `low_mood`. `claim_relies_mainly()` writes this
claim: each of the two predictors with the largest average PFI has at least twice the PFI of every other predictor.
It also records the six scope elements (quantity, model, procedure, data, meaning, and use) and that the claim was
formulated after the results were seen.

```{r claim-1}
claim1 = claim_relies_mainly(imp, k = 2, factor = 2, learners = "xgboost")
claim1
claim1$scope$quantity
```

## Steps 3 and 4: required properties and evidence

`csdg_check()` derives the properties that the claim requires from the gate plan and evaluates each with the default
criteria of the article. One property cannot be computed: whether the items measure what their names say, whether
the outcome was coded as intended, and which respondents the data cover (G0b, measurement and data). The data alone
do not show this, so the package leaves G0b open until the researcher judges it, here from the codebook and checks of
the data. The judgment is entered once and passed to every check of these data.

```{r check-1}
g0b = csdg_judge("G0b", supported(),
  note = "Items and outcome coded as in the codebook; no missing or out-of-range values.")
chk1 = csdg_check(claim1, imp, judgments = g0b)
chk1
```

Each row is one property with its gate, check, and status. Under G2, the content compares the averages over folds:
each named item is compared with every other item, and each margin, the PFI of the named item minus twice the PFI of
the other item, must hold beyond Monte Carlo error, with the lower bound of its corrected interval at or above the
smallest relevant difference; the observation reports the margins against the largest other item and the weakest of
all comparisons. The minimum importance compares each named item with 1% of the improvement, the procedure records
that the wording names marginal PFI, and the dependence screen reports how well the other predictors predict each
named item. Under G5, the selection is repeated in each fold: `r txt(chk1$details$stability$xgboost$n_holds)` of
`r txt(fits$K)` folds reproduce the claim. Held-out performance (G1) and ridge logistic regression (G6a) are context.
`print(chk1, details = TRUE)` adds each criterion and its relevance.

## Step 5: decision and report

```{r assess-1}
res1 = csdg_assess(chk1)
res1
```

```{r assert-1, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(res1$assessment, "met"))
```

The claim is `r txt(res1$label)`. Without the judgment of G0b, the same check would leave the claim unresolved. The
label "exploratory" records that the claim was formulated after the explanation was inspected; the data that suggested
it cannot also test it.

## Steps 1 to 5 for an order claim

XGBoost gives the two wordings of the worry item different PFI. Given the pair, `claim_order()` orders it by the
average PFI and writes the claim that XGBoost relies more on the first wording than on the second.

```{r claim-2}
claim2 = claim_order(imp, c("worry_a", "worry_b"), learners = "xgboost")
chk2_marginal = csdg_check(claim2, imp, judgments = g0b)
res2_marginal = csdg_assess(chk2_marginal)
res2_marginal
```

The other predictors predict each wording almost perfectly (R^2^ =
`r txt(sub("^0", "", num(chk2_marginal$details$dependence$r2[[1L]], 2L)))` in a linear regression on the other 11
items). Marginal PFI can
shift importance between such dependent predictors, so without a comparison that accounts for the dependence, the
claim faces an unresolved threat under G2 and is `r txt(res2_marginal$label)`. Conditional PFI permutes one wording
within the answers to the other, so the permuted inputs stay realistic. Passing the existing result to
`csdg_importance()` adds it; the marginal values do not change.

```{r claim-2-conditional, fig.alt = "Bar chart of marginal and conditional PFI of the two wordings of the worry item for each learner."}
imp2 = csdg_importance(imp, conditional = list(worry_a = "worry_b", worry_b = "worry_a"))
plot(imp2, features = c("worry_a", "worry_b"))
res2 = csdg_assess(csdg_check(claim2, imp2, judgments = g0b))
res2
```

```{r assert-2, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(res2_marginal$assessment, "unresolved"), res2$assessment %in% c("not_met", "unresolved"))
conditional_value = function(feature) {
  imp2$summary[learner == "xgboost" & type == "conditional" & feature_group == feature, mean_importance]
}
```

Once one wording is known, the other adds `r num(conditional_value(claim2$first), 2L)` (`r txt(claim2$first)`) and
`r num(conditional_value(claim2$second), 2L)` (`r txt(claim2$second)`) log-loss units. The claim is
`r txt(res2$label)` (decisive: `r txt(as.data.table(res2)$decisive_checks)`): neither wording adds information
beyond the other, so the order holds only under marginal permutation, which the wording does not name. With
`marginal_only = TRUE`, the claim would describe only marginal permutation. `csdg_loco()`, which refits the learners
without each predictor, measures the same information; claims derived from it are checked in the same way.

## Steps 1 to 5 for a direction

`csdg_effect()` computes the accumulated local effect (ALE) of predictors in the held-out folds and its change
between the 10th and the 90th percentile. After looking at it, `claim_direction()` writes the direction as a claim.

```{r direction}
eff = csdg_effect(fits, c("poor_sleep", "stress"))
eff
claim3 = claim_direction(eff, "poor_sleep", learners = "xgboost")
res3 = csdg_assess(csdg_check(claim3, eff, judgments = g0b))
res3
```

```{r direction-folds, include = FALSE}
st3 = res3$check$details$stability$xgboost
```

For "rise," the default criterion of the article also bounds the decrease between adjacent grid points: in each fold,
the change between the two percentiles must reach the minimum change, and no decrease of the ALE between adjacent grid
points in this range may exceed it. The held-out curves of XGBoost meet both conditions in
`r txt(st3$n_holds)` of `r txt(fits$K)` folds (largest decrease `r num(max(st3$folds$reversal), 2L)`), so the claim
is `r txt(res3$label)`. The claim that the predictions are higher at the 90th than at the 10th percentile needs only
the change:

```{r direction-higher}
claim4 = claim_direction(eff, "poor_sleep", learners = "xgboost", monotone = FALSE)
res4 = csdg_assess(csdg_check(claim4, eff, judgments = g0b))
res4
```

This claim is `r txt(res4$label)`.

## Step 5 on new data

`csdg_confirm()` applies claim 1 with the criteria of `chk1` to a new sample from the same population. Given a new
task, it fits the same learners with the same resampling and seeds and computes PFI with the same settings; the two
predictors are not selected again, the criteria were fixed before the new data were analyzed, and the judgment of G0b
is carried over (pass `judgments` if the new data need their own). Rows of the new data that duplicate rows of the
original data give a warning with their number.

```{r confirm}
task_new = simulate_survey(1000L, seed = 1003L)
conf1 = csdg_confirm(chk1, task_new)
conf1
```

```{r assert-3, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(conf1$assessment, "met"))
```

Claim 1 is `r txt(conf1$label)`.

## Step 5: report every claim checked

The article asks researchers to report every claim they checked, not only those that were met. The package logs
each derived claim and each check, assessment, and test on new data of the session; `csdg_export_assessment()` writes
the log with the records of an assessment, without models, predictions, or row-level data.

```{r records}
csdg_claim_log()[function_name %in% c("csdg_assess", "csdg_confirm"), .(statement, result)]
list.files(csdg_export_assessment(res1, tempdir()))
```

`as.data.table(chk1)` holds the full property, criterion, observation, and relevance of each row, and
`chk1$records` holds the evidence records. The numerical example of the article is worked through in
`vignette("claim_scoped_diagnostic_gates", package = "mlr3autoiml")`, and the
[function reference](https://stefancoors.de/mlr3autoiml/reference/index.html) documents all arguments and criteria.
